cues.text: Section two: the eight components of an IT strategy.
Let us take them one at a time, beginning with business alignment.
Business alignment means understanding customer needs, market conditions, the organisation's mission and its internal capabilities.
Once you understand these, you translate each priority into an investment that has a named business owner and a measurable outcome.
Consider a bank that seeks financial inclusion.
It might prioritise low-bandwidth mobile services rather than an expensive desktop-only application, because the first serves the customers it actually wants to reach.
The second component is enterprise architecture, abbreviated EA.
EA is a blueprint that connects business processes to the technology that supports them.
It has four parts.
Business architecture describes capabilities and workflows.
Application architecture describes software and how those applications interact.
Data architecture describes information, its ownership and its flows.
And technology architecture describes networks, compute, storage and platforms.
Two well-known frameworks support this work.
TOGAF provides an architecture development approach, while Zachman provides a classification structure for architectural descriptions.
Here is an example.
A hospital may have separate billing, clinical and pharmacy systems.
EA can be used to identify duplicated patient records, incompatible interfaces, and opportunities for shared identity and integration.
Notice that architecture is not merely a network diagram.
It connects technology choices to business capabilities.
The third component is governance.
Governance defines who makes decisions, how investments are approved, how risks are escalated, and who is accountable.
Management, by contrast, executes those decisions.
A steering committee involving finance, operations, IT and business leadership can prevent departments from independently buying incompatible systems.
Fourth is application portfolio management.
Here you maintain an inventory of software, and assess each application's business value, technical fitness, costs, risks and duplication.
Gartner's TIME model classifies applications into four categories.
Tolerate means retain the application for now.
Invest means enhance valuable, healthy systems.
Migrate means move systems that are valuable but technically unsuitable.
Eliminate means retire systems that are low in value and unsuitable.
For instance, a legacy billing application may have high business value but poor maintainability.
In that case, migration is preferable to abrupt retirement.
Fifth is data strategy and analytics.
A data strategy defines how information is collected, stored, integrated, secured, governed and used.
One term to know is ETL, which means extract, transform and load.
Data is retrieved from source systems, cleaned or converted, and then loaded into a target store.
On the analytics side, there are three levels.
Dashboards describe what happened.
Predictive analytics estimates what may happen.
Prescriptive analytics recommends actions.
Poor-quality inputs undermine all three.
Sixth is cybersecurity strategy.
This involves identifying threats and vulnerabilities, assessing risk, establishing controls, planning incident response and recovery, and meeting privacy obligations.
Encryption, access control, backups and monitoring are complementary, meaning they work together rather than substituting for one another.
Nigerian data protection obligations must be considered when handling personal data, and European GDPR requirements may apply in relevant circumstances.
Security is also a business enabler, because customers and regulators must trust the service.
Seventh is human capital development.
Technology creates little value without competent people.
So you assess skill gaps, train staff, develop career pathways, plan succession, and build a culture of continuous learning.
Introducing ERP without training may simply produce expensive software sitting alongside the old spreadsheets.
The eighth and final component is budgeting and ROI.
Here you estimate acquisition, integration, operation, training, maintenance and retirement costs.
Total cost of ownership, or TCO, includes costs across the whole lifecycle.
Return on investment, or ROI, compares net benefit with investment.
The formula is: ROI equals benefits minus costs, divided by costs, multiplied by one hundred percent.
